definition: Arbitration hearings are the equivalent of a courtroom trial, but less formal. During hearings, all parties meet to hear the case and to present supporting evidence. Usually, hearings begin with a brief statement by the panel, followed by opening statements from each party. Then, the claimant may present their case, including evidence, witness testimony, and experts. The opposing party has a chance to cross-examine all the witnesses presented. Then the roles reverse. The respondent may present their evidence and witnesses, leaving the claimant a chance to cross-examine these witnesses. Unlike a trial, the panel may pose questions to the witnesses at any point to clarify any issues. Some testimony may even be taken by phone, depending on the availability and the potential costs for causing a witness to appear before the panel of arbitrators. Finally, each party offers their closing argument and the panel goes into deliberations. The Federal Rules of Evidence (e.g., hearsay and admissibility of evidence) that operate in the courtroom do not operate to the same extent in arbitration. Arbitrators tend to be much more flexible than judges in allowing evidence to come in. According to the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority (FINRA), while arbitration may take up to 16 months, most hearings tend to last about four days. Their informal nature allows for flexibility in the schedule and presentation of evidence. However, hearing fees are calculated per day, making a lengthier arbitration much more costly than a shorter one. In sum, a FINRA hearing typically proceeds according to the following timeline:  Swearing in of arbitrators, parties, and witnesses;  Opening statement from each party;  Claimants’ presentation of facts of the case to arbitrators, including testimony;  Respondents’ presentation of facts of the case to arbitrators, including testimony;  Presentation of any counter-claims, cross-claims, or third-party claims;  Rebuttal evidence;  Closing statements;  Scheduling post-hearing submissions before closing the record; and  Arbitration panel closes the record.
